The teenager had joined the student demonstrations that forced the former Education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Like many young protesters around her, she directed her ire at Prime Minister Narendra Modi. A video clip of her comments went viral. Then came the targeted harassment campaign. Leading the charge was an organisation called The Jaipur Dialogues. Founded by Sanjay Dixit, a former Indian Administrative Services officer, it describes itself as a “vibrant online platform that aims to promote Indic knowledge systems.” In a series of posts on X, The Jaipur Dialogues’ handle sought the girl’s identifying details, branded her “most wanted”, and eventually, doxxed her. items.title: The GenZ effect: Why the future of law looks different
items.summary: Individuals born between 1997 and 2012 - often called Gen Z or Zoomers - are redefining norms, behaviours and expectations among the entire global legal fraternity. Law is actively shaped by the social and technological realities of a new era and today, Gen Z is doing it with their pragmatism, inclusivity and tech-savviness. They are often solution-oriented and exhibit a practical approach in tackling societal issues. This generation enters the legal profession with a deep-rooted belief that law should actually work for people. The ethos that GenZ is expected to bring to the field centres on socially conscious legal advocacy, digital fluency, work/life balance and an end to the rigid, often absurd hierarchies that still define legal practice. With this shift, the methods, expectations and values shaping law are being reinterpreted, paving the way for more diversity, innovation and authenticity in the profession. GenZ and the politics of accountability Today, law is regarded as more than a symbol of prestige, wealth, or corporate dominance. A Division Bench of Justice Saumitra Dayal Singh and Justice Swarupama Chaturvedi declared Sections 8, 9, 10, 38 and 42 of the Act ultra vires. The Court held that Sections 8, 9 and 10 – which pertain to payment of rent and its revision - were repugnant to the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. “As to the rent payable, Section 8 allows that revision of the same in terms of Section 9 and for its determination in terms of Section 10. Also, Section 10 provides for determination of revised rent in the case of the dispute between the landlord and the tenant i.e. lessor and lessee that is completely in conflict with the provisions of TPA,” the Bench observed. items.title: Rs 428 crore in, Rs 1 crore out: How Chinese capital and public money vanished into Gurugram’s garbage
items.summary: Start at the end. In the summer of 2024, a Chinese firm that runs waste-to-energy plants sold its entire Indian business for Rs 1 crore – about the price of a modest flat in the city it had been hired to clean. Seven years earlier it had bought that same business, pumped in roughly Rs 428 crore, and promised to shrink the growing landfills in Gurugram and Faridabad. Somewhere between the Rs 428 crore that went in and the Rs 1 crore that came out is the story of too many backers disappointed. And it is not a simple one, of an Indian company taking foreign investors for a ride. This is the story of that Indian firm, Ecogreen Energy Pvt Ltd, failing to deliver the Indian expansion that China Jinjiang Environment Holding Co Ltd had made it the anchor of. It is the story of a web of firms linked to Ecogreen – some the promoters’ own – in effect absorbing money meant for waste plants and garbage processing into consultancy fees, rent and inside deals. items.summary: Karnataka has recorded 4,212 laboratory-confirmed influenza cases across 32 districts so far this year, with the Health Department attributing the current rise in H1N1 cases to the state’s usual seasonal pattern and urging people not to panic. According to surveillance data from the Integrated Health Information Platform (IHIP), 4,212 influenza cases had been confirmed in the state as of August 22, 2026. H1N1 is a strain of the influenza A virus that can cause seasonal flu. Common symptoms include fever, cough, sore throat, body ache and fatigue. Bengaluru accounts for the majority of the cases. The Greater Bengaluru Authority (MSU) area has reported 2,070 cases so far this year, compared to 2,587 in 2025 and 1,189 in 2024. Bengaluru Urban has recorded 1,011 cases, broadly comparable to 961 cases in 2025 and 991 in 2024. The Health Department said influenza generally records two seasonal peaks in Karnataka — between January and March and again between July and September.
